opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for me the exciting part was that it pointed to a genuinely new axis for scaling. For years the story was mostly about scaling pre-training: more data, more parameters, more compute up front. With o1, OpenAI showed that you can also get big gains by spending more compute at inference time, letting the model think longer before it answers. And they had these plots where performance on hard math and reasoning benchmarks kept climbing as you gave the model more thinking budget. That's a really compelling picture, because it suggests capability isn't fixed once training ends.

At the same time, it was frustrating from a research perspective, because they didn't really tell us how they did it. There was a lot of speculation about elaborate reinforcement learning pipelines, search, process reward models, all sorts of complicated machinery. So the question that got me excited was: what's the simplest possible way to get this behavior? Do you actually need all that complexity, or can you get test-time scaling with something much more minimal?

That's really what motivated our work on s1. We found that with a small, carefully curated set of reasoning examples, around a thousand high-quality questions with reasoning traces, plus a very simple trick for controlling how long the model thinks at inference, you can reproduce a lot of that scaling behavior. The trick, which we called budget forcing, either cuts the thinking off or, if you want it to think more, suppresses the end-of-thinking token and appends something like "Wait," which nudges the model to keep going and often catch its own mistakes.

So o1 was exciting partly for what it showed, and partly for the open question it left, which was whether this could be made simple, transparent, and accessible to the open research community. I think the answer turned out to be yes, at least to a surprising degree.

r001.rationale: The candidate says o1’s performance on hard math and reasoning benchmarks kept climbing as it was given more thinking budget at inference time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think what was exciting about o1 was that it showed, very clearly, that you can get a lot of performance gains from scaling test-time compute. So up to that point, most of the progress in the field had really come from scaling training compute, right, scaling up the data, scaling up the model size, and then you get a better model. And what o1 showed is that there's this whole other axis, where you take a model and at inference time you let it think for longer, generate these long reasoning chains, and the performance on things like math and coding goes up a lot, and it goes up in this fairly predictable way where the more you let it think, the better it gets.

And I think what made it really interesting as a research direction is that they didn't really say how they did it. So you had this very strong result, and this plot showing that accuracy improves with test-time compute, but the recipe was not public. And so for us, the natural question was, what's the simplest way to get this behavior? Do you need a lot of reinforcement learning, do you need huge amounts of data, or can you actually get there with something much more minimal? And that's kind of what motivated the s1 work, where we wanted to see if you could take an off-the-shelf model, fine-tune it on a very small, carefully curated set of reasoning traces, and then control the amount of thinking at test time with something very simple, like just forcing the model to keep going. And it turned out you could get pretty far with that, which I think says something about how much of this capability is already latent in the pretrained models.

r001.rationale: The response says o1 showed performance gains from scaling test-time compute and that accuracy improved as the model was allowed to think longer.

That opens up some really interesting research questions. How do you train a model to use that extra compute productively? How much does more thinking actually help? And can you get a smaller model to solve harder problems by giving it more time? That felt like a very promising dimension to explore.

Instead of getting better results only by training a larger model, you can let the model spend more time reasoning through a difficult problem. That opens up a whole set of research questions: how do you train that behavior, how do you decide when more reasoning is useful, and how much improvement can you get from that extra compute?
